cf.title: Add support for INSERT ... SET syntax

input.subject: [PATCH] Add support for INSERT ... SET syntax

verdict_reasoning: The single-row form has lasting demand and no surviving objection. The parenthesized multi-row form has no shown demand (demand-1) and no comparison with Oracle 23 or a draft standard text, while MariaDB spells it differently (prior-attempts-1). Its indirection rule turns an internal shared column list into a user-visible syntax rule (standards-compat-2). The list should settle the multi-row form before code review.

brief.title: Add insert ... set syntax with named column assignments
brief.problem: In insert, the column list sits apart from the values. With many columns, or when only some columns get values, the reader must match names to values by position. The author wants a form that keeps each column name next to its value.
brief.proposed_design: insert gains a SET clause as one more alternative to VALUES, DEFAULT VALUES and a query: `set col=expr, ...` for one row, or `set (col=expr, ...), (...)` for several rows. Rows may name different columns, columns are matched by name, and omitted columns get their default. In multi-row form, an array-element or subfield target must be identical in every row that touches that column, because all rows share one column list.
user_visible_surface: New insert syntax: `insert into t set col=expr | DEFAULT [, ...]`, which cannot be combined with an explicit column list.
New multi-row form: `insert into t set (col=expr, ...), (col=expr, ...)`, where rows may list different columns.
Subfield and array-element targets (`c.x=1`, `arr[1]=1`). A repeated identical target in one row fails with "column ... specified more than once", which column-list insert accepts.
New error when rows of a multi-row SET disagree on an indirection target for the same column.
psql tab completion of SET and of column names after SET.
author_claims: SET syntax is more readable than a separate column list and VALUES, mainly for single-row inserts of some columns.
Works with DEFAULT, expressions, subqueries, RETURNING, ON CONFLICT and OVERRIDING { SYSTEM | USER } VALUE.
Rejecting repeated identical targets ensures no assigned expression is silently discarded.
Andrew Dunstan says Oracle 23 has this syntax and a proposal may exist to add it to the SQL standard.
brief.thread_state: David Johnston gave -1 to inventing a variant insert syntax, Tom Lane pointed to earlier unadopted proposals, and Álvaro Herrera linked threads from 2016 and 2019. Reviewers then found a crash and array-target bugs that v7 addresses; Peter Eisentraut is the listed committer but has not posted, and Mario Gonzalez asks whether any committer supports it.
unclear: No reply addresses the -1 from David Johnston or explains why the 2016 and 2019 proposals were not adopted.
The proposal does not say whether its syntax matches the Oracle form or the possible SQL standard text, for example the parenthesized multi-row form.
The proposal does not say whether SET becomes a more reserved keyword or causes grammar conflicts.
The proposal does not say how SET relates to the INSERT BY NAME variant Andrew Dunstan plans to submit.
The proposal does not say how ruleutils and pg_dump print views or rules that use the new form.

prior_attempts.title: Implement INSERT SET syntax
prior_attempts.quote: This patch has been basically ignored for a full two years now.
prior_attempts.reason: The patch got too little reviewer and committer interest. Tom Lane noted it had been ignored for two years, and the commitfest manager returned it because no one took up the review. Earlier concerns from Tom Lane and Peter are mentioned, but their messages are not shown.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P2 also offered an optional FROM clause that turned the insert into INSERT ... SELECT. This patch drops FROM and adds a parenthesized multi-row form in which rows may name different columns.

prior_attempts.title: SET syntax for INSERT
prior_attempts.what_is_different: The row records no design detail and no reason, so the material does not show how this proposal differs.

prior_attempts.title: MAP syntax for arrays
prior_attempts.who_objected: Tom Lane, Andreas Karlsson, Ashutosh Bapat
prior_attempts.quote: Yeah, it's a handy syntax, but it's not that much better than using a subselect or a writing a user-defined function. And there's risk of future conflicts with the SQL standard.
prior_attempts.reason: Reviewers objected to adding proprietary syntax that could conflict with future SQL standard use of the MAP keyword, which is already a non-reserved keyword in SQL:2016. They also judged the syntax not much better than the existing sub-select with unnest and array_agg, which is more flexible (for example, it allows a WHERE filter), and suggested optimizing the unnest/array_agg combination in the planner instead of adding new syntax. Heikki Linnakangas summarized the consensus as not wanting the feature and marked the entry Rejected.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P11 proposed different syntax (MAP over arrays) with no implementation elsewhere. Its concern about non-standard syntax that may conflict with a later standard applies here mainly to the multi-row form.

objections.title: Multi-row SET form may diverge from a future SQL standard
objections.failure_scenario: Users write `insert ... set (a=1), (b=2)` in application code after release. If the standard later adopts a different multi-row form, such as MariaDB's repeated SET, Postgres must either carry two spellings forever or break those statements.
objections.argument: Message #4 says only that a standard proposal may exist, and nothing in the thread compares the patch's grammar with that text or with the Oracle form. Message #19 shows MariaDB already uses repeated SET for several rows, while this patch uses parenthesized groups, so the multi-row shape is not settled elsewhere. [P11] was rejected partly for the "risk of future conflicts with the SQL standard". Message #2 objects to Postgres inventing its own insert variant, and no reply answers that.
objections.author_must_show: Does the parenthesized multi-row form match Oracle 23 or the draft standard text, and if not, why not limit the patch to the single-row form?

critic.reasoning: No message compares `set (...), (...)` with the Oracle form or a draft standard text, and message #19 reports a different multi-row spelling in MariaDB. [P11] concerned a new keyword with no prior implementation elsewhere, so it gives only weak support.

objections.title: Same SET spelling follows different rules in insert and update
objections.failure_scenario: A user copies `set arr[1]=1, arr[1]=2` from an update into an insert ... set and gets "specified more than once". A multi-row insert where one row omits a column that another row assigns as `arr[1]` fails, while a single-row insert with the same omission succeeds, so the user cannot predict which statements work.
objections.argument: The v7 commit message says the duplicate rule is deliberately stricter than column-list insert and update. Message #20 adds a multi-row rule that exists only because rows share one column list internally. The user sees an internal parse-analysis shape as a syntax rule, a departure from existing practice that needs justification. A standard text may later define these cases differently.
objections.author_must_show: Why should insert ... set reject repeats that update ... set accepts, and what do Oracle or the standard proposal do in both cases?

critic.reasoning: The commit message justifies the duplicate-target rule, so that half is answered. The multi-row rule stands: message #20 says it exists because rows share one column list, so users see an internal limit as a syntax rule.

objections.title: Multi-row set form has no shown demand and matches no cited system
objections.failure_scenario: A user ports a MariaDB multi-row insert that repeats SET per row and gets a syntax error. A later SQL standard or Oracle text may define multi-row SET differently. Postgres would then carry a parenthesized form that nobody asked for and that conflicts with the standard one.
objections.argument: The demand shown in the thread covers the single-row form: Oracle 23 (message #4), MySQL and MariaDB (message #19), and the 2016 and 2019 proposals (message #5). Message #19 reports that MySQL allows only one row and that MariaDB repeats SET for each row, which differs from `set (...), (...)`. No message shows that Oracle or the possible standard text uses the parenthesized form. Its restrictions on indirection targets, and the new error, exist only because of this form (messages #19, #20).
objections.author_must_show: Which existing system or draft standard text uses `set (col=expr, ...), (...)` for multi-row insert, and which users have asked for that form?

critic.reasoning: The demand in messages #4, #5 and #19 covers the single-row form; no message names a system or user request for `set (...), (...)`. Messages #19 and #20 confirm that the indirection restrictions come from this form alone.

refuted.title: Multi-row SET spelling may not match Oracle or a future standard
refuted.failure_scenario: Postgres ships `set (a=1, b=2), (a=3)`. The standard, or Oracle's existing form, then uses a different multi-row spelling, such as MariaDB's repeated SET. Postgres must keep its own form forever beside the standard one, and users porting from Oracle find statements that do not parse.
refuted.argument: The case for the feature in message #4 rests on Oracle 23 having it and a possible standard proposal, but no message compares the patch grammar with either. Message #19 shows MariaDB spells multi-row SET differently, so the parenthesized form is one of several candidates. The objection in message #2, that Postgres should not invent its own insert variant, is not answered. [P11] was rejected partly for the risk of future conflicts with the SQL standard.
refuted.author_must_show: Does each form, single-row and parenthesized multi-row, match the Oracle 23 syntax or the draft standard text, and where does it differ?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of prior-attempts-1, which states the same multi-row divergence risk and adds a concrete way out (limit the patch to the single-row form).

refuted.title: Two non-positional insert forms proposed separately, with no shared design
refuted.failure_scenario: SET is committed now, and INSERT BY NAME arrives in a later release from a separate patch. The two forms then disagree on defaults for omitted columns, duplicate targets or indirection. Users and documentation carry two non-standard ways to do the same job, each with its own rules.
refuted.argument: Message #4 says the Oracle feature includes both SET and BY NAME, and message #6 says a BY NAME patch will follow separately. The proposal does not say how the two forms relate or share rules. Each form adds a permanent grammar alternative to insert.
refuted.author_must_show: How will insert ... set and insert by name share rules for omitted columns, duplicates and indirection, and should they be designed together?

critic.reasoning: The scenario depends on an INSERT BY NAME patch that is not yet submitted, and no concrete rule conflict is named. Message #6 shows its author knows this patch and chose to submit BY NAME separately.

refuted.title: SET form designed without the planned BY NAME variant or standard text
refuted.failure_scenario: The parenthesized multi-row `set (...), (...)` form ships in a release. Later the SQL standard, or the INSERT BY NAME patch, defines non-positional insert differently, for example by repeating SET per row as MariaDB does. Postgres then has to keep both grammars or break users.
refuted.argument: Message #4 says Oracle 23 has this syntax and a standard proposal may exist, and message #6 says a separate INSERT BY NAME patch is coming. The proposal does not compare its multi-row form with Oracle or with any draft text. Message #19 shows that other systems use a different multi-row form. In [P11], reviewers turned down handy syntax because of the risk of future conflict with the standard, and that risk applies here.
refuted.author_must_show: Does the single-row and multi-row grammar match the Oracle 23 form and any draft standard text, and how will INSERT BY NAME fit beside it?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of prior-attempts-1 on the multi-row form. The BY NAME part repeats standards-compat-3 and has the same speculative scenario.

refuted.title: A second insert path with its own target rules to maintain
refuted.failure_scenario: A later patch changes how column-list INSERT handles indirection targets, defaults or OVERRIDING. It updates the VALUES path, and transformInsertSetClause() keeps the old rules. Users find out when the two forms of the same insert behave differently, and no test fails.
refuted.argument: v7 states that SET is stricter than column-list INSERT on repeated targets. It also adds multi-row rules on indirection that VALUES does not have (message #20, message #23). Each later INSERT feature must now decide its behaviour in two places, and the rules already differ. Three review rounds found a crash and silent misassignment in this one area (message #7, message #15), which shows how easy it is to get this path wrong.
refuted.author_must_show: Could SET be rewritten into the existing column-list form so it reuses one path, and why do its rules differ from column-list INSERT?

critic.reasoning: Messages #18 and #20 say SET is merged into one shared column list and then goes through the existing transformAssignedExpr() and rewriter code. Defaults and OVERRIDING are handled in that shared code; the rule differences are covered by standards-compat-2.

refuted.title: No committer has engaged after three CommitFests
refuted.failure_scenario: The patch goes in with core grammar and parse-analysis changes, and its only reviewers were colleagues from one company. A bug report on views, rules or ON CONFLICT with SET then arrives, and no committer who has studied the design can answer it.
refuted.argument: Message #22 asks whether any committer sponsors the patch. The listed committer has not posted in 23 messages. The -1 in message #2 and the question in message #3 about why earlier attempts failed got no answer. [P2] was returned because it drew no review or committer interest for two years. This point concerns committability more than merit.
refuted.author_must_show: Which committer has reviewed the grammar and analysis design and is willing to own later fixes?

critic.reasoning: Peter Eisentraut added himself as committer on the CommitFest entry, and Andrew Dunstan posted support and helped with v2 (messages #4, #8). The objection itself says it concerns committability, which the rubric keeps apart from the verdict.

refuted.title: Column-list insert already does this; the gain is readability only
refuted.failure_scenario: A user who writes `insert into users (name, email, status) values (...)` gets the same row as with `insert into users set name=..., ...`. Postgres then keeps two grammars for one result in gram.y, analyze.c, psql and the docs. The rules for repeated and indirection targets already differ between the two, so every later insert change must cover both.
refuted.argument: The commit message calls SET "a more convenient and readable alternative" and does not name a statement that column-list insert cannot express. The proposal adds no new capability, so it is a permanent addition made only for convenience. Message #2 gives -1 to a variant insert syntax, and no later message answers it. In [P11], handy proprietary syntax that was "not that much better" than the existing way was rejected.
refuted.author_must_show: Which inserts can SET express that a column list with VALUES cannot, and is readability alone enough to justify a second insert grammar?

critic.reasoning: Message #4 answers the -1 by pointing to Oracle 23, and message #5 lists independent proposals from 2016 and 2019 plus a user request. That is lasting demand from several sources; [P11] was syntax with no implementation elsewhere.

refuted.title: Second by-name insert form planned in parallel with INSERT BY NAME
refuted.failure_scenario: SET ships with its parenthesized multi-row form, rows that may name different columns, and its own indirection rules. INSERT BY NAME, or a later standard text, then arrives with other rules for omitted columns and per-row shape. Users and later patches face two by-name insert mechanisms with semantics that cannot be aligned without breaking one of them.
refuted.argument: In message #4 and message #6, a WIP INSERT BY NAME patch is said to be coming, and Oracle's version is said to ship both forms. The proposal does not say how SET and BY NAME share matching rules or analysis code. Message #19 notes that MariaDB writes multi-row SET as repeated SET clauses, while this patch uses parenthesized rows. Once the multi-row shape ships, Postgres cannot take it back.
refuted.author_must_show: How do SET and the planned INSERT BY NAME share one by-name matching mechanism, and does the multi-row form match Oracle's form or the possible standard text?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of prior-attempts-1 on the multi-row form. The BY NAME part names no concrete rule conflict, as in standards-compat-3.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: The patch changes the raw InsertStmt node in parsenodes.h and adds handling in nodeFuncs.c.

touch_points.label: SQL-standard conflict or non-standard syntax
touch_points.reason: The patch adds a SET alternative to insert, with a parenthesized multi-row form not compared with Oracle or the standard.

touch_points.label: pg_dump / restore round-trip
touch_points.reason: The proposal does not say how ruleutils and pg_dump print rules that use insert ... set.

touch_points.label: psql UX conventions
touch_points.reason: The patch adds psql tab completion of SET and of column names after SET.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: A permanent second spelling of insert in gram.y and analyze.c, with duplicate and indirection rules that differ from column-list insert.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Do the single-row form and the parenthesized multi-row form match the Oracle 23 syntax and any draft SQL standard text, and where do they differ?
Which existing system or user request uses `set (col=expr, ...), (...)`, and if none, why not limit the patch to the single-row form?
Why must every row of a multi-row SET use the same subfield or subscript target, and can the patch remove that rule instead of documenting it?
Does the patch change the keyword class of SET or add grammar conflicts in gram.y?
How do ruleutils and pg_dump print a rule whose action uses insert ... set?

committability.owner_note: A committer who knows gram.y and insert parse analysis must own it. Andrew Dunstan posted support and helped with v2; the committer listed on the CommitFest entry has not posted in the thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the insert ... set grammar permanently, including the multi-row form and its indirection rules, even if a later SQL standard text spells them differently.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted seven versions through message #23 and fixed the crash and the array-target bugs that reviewers reported.

priority.reason: The single-row form has demand from three Postgres proposals since 2016 and from Oracle 23, MySQL and MariaDB. The multi-row form needs a comparison with Oracle and the standard, or removal, before a review of the 49 KiB grammar and analysis patch is worth the time.

provisional_note: Without the code, this review could not check grammar conflicts, the keyword class of SET, or how stored rules that use the new form deparse. Only 3 of 23 messages were read directly.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.summary: SET syntax for INSERT

precedents_retrieved.title: Implement INSERT SET syntax
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a SET clause to INSERT, so columns and values are written in pairs as in UPDATE, with an optional FROM clause to take values from other relations such as a CTE. The grammar turns INSERT SET into an INSERT with VALUES, or with a SELECT when FROM is used.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch got too little reviewer and committer interest. Tom Lane noted it had been ignored for two years, and the commitfest manager returned it because no one took up the review. Earlier concerns from Tom Lane and Peter are mentioned, but their messages are not shown.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: This patch has been basically ignored for a full two years now.

precedents_retrieved.title: Parallel INSERT (INTO ... SELECT ...)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set allows parallel execution of both the INSERT and the SELECT parts of "INSERT INTO ... SELECT ...", with workers inserting tuples themselves; where parallel insert is unsafe (for example foreign keys or ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE), only the SELECT part is parallelised. It changes the planner, executor and parallel-worker code, adds parallel-safety checks on the target table (including partitions, triggers and domains), and adds a GUC and a reloption to control the feature.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Parts of the work, "Parallel SELECT for INSERT" and the related GUC/reloption, were committed during the thread. The remaining patches, which add the parallel INSERT functionality itself, were marked Returned with Feedback because of feedback given on pgsql-committers, which said a lot of work remained. The visible messages do not show the content of that feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
There is a lot of work
to do for this patch as per the feedback given on pgsql-committers
[1].

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Enable parallel SELECT for "INSERT INTO ... SELECT ..."."
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Enable parallel SELECT for "INSERT INTO ... SELECT ..."."
Reverted commit(s): Doc: Update description for parallel insert reloption.; Add a new GUC and a reloption to enable inserts in parallel-mode.; Improve FK trigger parallel-safety check added by 05c8482f7f.; Enable parallel SELECT for "INSERT INTO ... SELECT ...".; Fix use of relcache TriggerDesc field introduced by commit 05c8482f7f.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
To allow inserts in parallel-mode this feature has to ensure that all the
constraints, triggers, etc. are parallel-safe for the partition hierarchy
which is costly and we need to find a better way to do that. Additionally,
we could have used existing cached information in some cases like indexes,
domains, etc. to determine the parallel-safety.

List of commits reverted, in reverse chronological order:

ed62d3737c Doc: Update description for parallel insert reloption.
c8f78b6161 Add a new GUC and a reloption to enable inserts in parallel-mode.
c5be48f092 Improve FK trigger parallel-safety check added by 05c8482f7f.
e2cda3c20a Fix use of relcache TriggerDesc field introduced by commit 05c8482f7f.
e4e87a32cc Fix valgrind issue in commit 05c8482f7f.

precedents_retrieved.title: In INSERT/UPDATE, use the table's real tuple descriptor as target.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
In INSERT/UPDATE, use the table's real tuple descriptor as target.
Reverted commit(s): Fix corner case for a BEFORE ROW UPDATE trigger returning OLD.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Previously, ExecInitModifyTable relied on ExecInitJunkFilter,
and thence ExecCleanTypeFromTL, to build the target descriptor from
the query tlist.  While we just checked (in ExecCheckPlanOutput)
that the tlist produces compatible output, this is not a great
substitute for the relation's actual tuple descriptor that's
available from the relcache.  For one thing, dropped columns will
not be correctly marked attisdropped; it's a bit surprising that
we've gotten away with that this long.  But the real reason for
being concerned with this is that using the table's descriptor means
that the slot will have correct attrmissing data, allowing us to
revert the klugy fix of commit ba9f18abd.  (This commit undoes
that one's changes in trigger.c, but keeps the new test case.)
Thus we can solve the bogus-trigger-tuple problem with fewer cycles
rather than more.

No back-patch, since this doesn't fix any additional bug, and it
seems somewhat more likely to have unforeseen side effects than
ba9f18abd's narrow fix.

precedents_retrieved.title: INSERT SELECT: BulkInsertState and table_multi_insert
precedents_retrieved.summary: Make INSERT, including INSERT SELECT and INSERT ... ON CONFLICT, use a BulkInsertState ring buffer as COPY does, so data loaders do not leave many dirty buffers in shared buffers. Later versions added a GUC to opt in, and switched to table_multi_insert after a set number of tuples.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The thread stalled. The multi-insert part became complex: it cannot handle volatile column defaults, and the author proposed leaving it to the separate "New Table Access Methods for Multi and Single Inserts" patch. The author split off the simple BulkInsertState patch and said to close the entry if no one was interested in it alone. No reviewer took that patch up, so the commitfest manager proposed closing it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Since the thread has stalled, maybe that's the best course of action here.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add SQL syntax check
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a --syntax option to the postgres server binary that reads SQL from standard input, runs it through the raw parser only (no catalog access or parse analysis), and reports whether it is valid SQL via a message and exit code. The intent was to support manual and automated script checks and editor integrations.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Several reviewers held that the feature did not belong in the postgres binary, and Robert Haas marked the entry Rejected on that basis. The main objection, attributed to Tom Lane and endorsed by Robert Haas, was that the check exposes an implementation detail, the division of work between gram.y (raw_parser) and parse analysis, so it would miss things users consider syntax errors and flag things that seem semantic. Making that work would need a much larger effort and a different design. Robert Haas also noted that the 45-line patch had no comments, tests or documentation, and the author agreed to the rejection.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I strongly suspect that doing something useful in this area requires
about two orders of magnitude more code than are included in this
patch, and a completely different design.

precedents_retrieved.title: Making autovacuum logs indicate if insert-based threshold was the triggering condition
precedents_retrieved.summary: Making autovacuum logs indicate if insert-based threshold was the triggering condition

precedents_retrieved.title: Ltree syntax improvement
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch extends the set of characters allowed in ltree labels by adding two escaping mechanisms, backslash-escaping of individual characters and double-quoting of whole labels, for the ltree, lquery and ltxtquery datatypes. Later versions refactored the label parsing into common code shared by the three types.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected to the design of having both quoting and backslash-escaping and proposed SQL-identifier-style quoting instead. He also questioned the stripping of leading and trailing whitespace, the structure of ltree_io.c (several routines that depend on the quoting rules and must stay in sync, plus multiple passes over the input), and changes to error reporting. After a later request to rebase, no new version was submitted for two months, and Michael Paquier marked the entry returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
As I mentioned upthread, I'm not convinced that we ought to have
*both* quoting and backslash-escaping in these datatypes.

precedents_retrieved.title: MAP syntax for arrays
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Tom Lane, Andreas Karlsson, Ashutosh Bapat
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a new expression type and syntax MAP(<func_name> OVER <array_expression>) that applies a function to each element of an array and returns the resulting array, reusing the existing array-coercion infrastructure. The author also considered a more general form mapping an arbitrary expression over an array, and reported better performance than the unnest/array_agg subquery approach for small arrays.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers objected to adding proprietary syntax that could conflict with future SQL standard use of the MAP keyword, which is already a non-reserved keyword in SQL:2016. They also judged the syntax not much better than the existing sub-select with unnest and array_agg, which is more flexible (for example, it allows a WHERE filter), and suggested optimizing the unnest/array_agg combination in the planner instead of adding new syntax. Heikki Linnakangas summarized the consensus as not wanting the feature and marked the entry Rejected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Yeah, it's a
handy syntax, but it's not that much better than using a subselect or a
writing a user-defined function. And there's risk of future conflicts
with the SQL standard.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow self-conflicting INSERT INTO .. ON CONFLICT DO UPDATEs
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE accept a command whose own proposed rows conflict with each other, as DO NOTHING already does. Today such a command fails with "command cannot affect row a second time".
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund and Peter Geoghegan voted against it, and the CFM returned it citing those two votes. Andres Freund objected that the patch makes one command update a row it inserted, producing cmin == cmax and breaking heap visibility rules. The author then found visibility bugs in his own patch. Peter Geoghegan argued that updating the same row twice in one command is not desirable and asked who would want it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: To me it seems as if allowing the same command to update the same row more than once is just not desirable in general.

precedents_retrieved.title: [PROPOSAL] : Disallow use of empty column name in (column_name '') in ALTER or CREATE of foreign table.
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes postgres_fdw's validator reject empty values for the column_name, schema_name and table_name options in create or alter foreign table. Today an empty column_name is accepted, and the remote query then fails with a zero-length identifier error.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane judged that the check did not add enough ease-of-use to justify the extra code, and he compared an empty name to a misspelled remote name, which cannot be checked either. Robert Haas pointed out that existing foreign tables with empty values would then fail pg_dump or pg_upgrade. Nobody argued for the patch after Tom voted against it, so Robert marked it Rejected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I was down on it to start with, on the grounds that it wasn't adding enough ease-of-use to justify even a relatively small amount of added code.

Revert MERGE patch
Reverted commit(s): MERGE SQL Command following SQL:2016; New files for MERGE; Improve parse representation for MERGE; MERGE syntax diagram correction; Allow cpluspluscheck to pass by renaming variable
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commits d204ef63776b8a00ca220adec23979091564e465,
83454e3c2b28141c0db01c7d2027e01040df5249 and a few more commits thereafter
(complete list at the end) related to MERGE feature.

While the feature was fully functional, with sufficient test coverage and
necessary documentation, it was felt that some parts of the executor and
parse-analyzer can use a different design and it wasn't possible to do that in
the available time. So it was decided to revert the patch for PG11 and retry
again in the future.

Thanks again to all reviewers and bug reporters.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Fix bogus %name-prefix option syntax in all our Bison files."
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Fix bogus %name-prefix option syntax in all our Bison files."
Reverted commit(s): Fix bogus %name-prefix option syntax in all our Bison files.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 45b7abe59e9485657ac9380f35d2d917dd0da25b.

It turns out that the %name-prefix syntax without "=" does not work
at all in pre-2.4 Bison.  We are not prepared to make such a large
jump in minimum required Bison version just to suppress a warning
message in a version hardly any developers are using yet.
When 3.0 gets more popular, we'll figure out a way to deal with this.
In the meantime, BISONFLAGS=-Wno-deprecated is recommendable for
anyone using 3.0 who doesn't want to see the warning.

roaster_notes.note: [P2] ended for lack of reviewer and committer interest, and [P1] has no recorded reason. In message #3 Tom Lane asked why the earlier attempts were not adopted, and message #5 links them, but no message reports the answer. That gap affects committability, not the merits.

The pg_dump and ruleutils round-trip was not raised. The new form likely becomes a normal insert during parse analysis, so a stored rule would print back as column-list syntax; checking this needs the code.

The patch adds no persistent or cross-node state. The touched files are gram.y, analyze.c, parsenodes.h and nodeFuncs.c, so INSERT ... SET is turned at parse analysis into an ordinary insert Query with a column list and VALUES. That leaves no change to WAL, the on-disk format, the catalogs or the wire protocol. Stored rules should deparse as plain insert ... values, but this could not be checked without the code. The new raw-node field in InsertStmt is a master-only change.

The proposal adds parser syntax that turns into an ordinary insert with a column list, so the existing table and column insert privileges, RLS policies and triggers apply unchanged; message #10 reports tests of column-level privilege violations. Nothing here creates a new privilege, default, exposure path or unbounded resource, so the security angle has no objection.
Two objections raised; no extension or external tool provides this, because it is grammar.

The single-row form has real demand: three Postgres proposals since 2016, an archive question from 2019, Oracle 23, MySQL and MariaDB. The earlier attempts [P1] [P2] stalled from lack of review, which is a committability issue rather than a demand issue.
